old: iron-bound with a wall that girds it
new: with an iron-bound wall that encircles it
reason: "girds" is an uncommon, archaic verb for "wraps around/encircles"; a listener unfamiliar with the word has nothing in the sentence to fall back on.

old: to hold the ways of the roaring winds
new: to hold the paths of the roaring winds
reason: "ways" meaning "routes/courses" is an archaic sense; on first hearing it more naturally reads as "manners/habits," which doesn't fit and forces a re-parse.

old: he could rouse or still each one of them as he pleased
new: he could stir up or calm each one of them as he pleased
reason: "still" used as a verb ("calm") is easy to mis-hear as the adverb "still" (yet), producing a momentary garden-path misread when listened to rather than read.

old: So they talked, and evil counsels won the day.
new: So they talked, and the bad idea won out.
reason: "evil counsels won the day" is a period idiom personifying abstract "counsels"; a modern listener has to work to connect it to "they gave in to the bad idea."

old: and this last answers the greeting
new: and the one leaving answers the greeting
reason: "this last" as a stand-in for "the latter" is a formal written construction, not spoken English, and is disorienting heard aloud without the option to reread.

old: a man who could do without sleep might earn double wages, one as a herdsman of cattle and another as a shepherd
new: a man who could do without sleep might earn double wages — one wage as a herdsman of cattle, another as a shepherd
reason: "one" and "another" immediately follow "a man," so a listener may briefly take them to mean two different men rather than two jobs held by the same man.

old: own sister to the magician Aeetes, for they are both children of the sun by Perse, who is daughter to Oceanus
new: own sister to the magician Aeetes — both of them children of the sun-god by the nymph Perse, daughter of Oceanus
reason: Three unfamiliar proper nouns (Aeetes, Perse, Oceanus) land in one clause with no signal of which (if any) matter later; a first-time listener can't register any of them before the sentence has moved on.

old: for the stag was much too big for me to carry on my shoulder, steadying him with one hand
new: for the stag was too big to carry on one shoulder — I had to steady him with one hand and lean on my spear with the other
reason: "steadying him with one hand" is left dangling after "leaning on my spear," so the listener has to work backward to figure out which hand is doing what; the physical picture briefly falls apart.

old: disguised as a young man in the first bloom of his youth and beauty, with the down just coming on his face
new: disguised as a young man in the first bloom of youth, with the first soft beard just showing on his face
reason: "the down" (fine new facial hair) is a homograph with the common word "down" (direction); heard aloud, "the down just coming on his face" can momentarily misread before the meaning resolves.

old: she will unman you and make you fit for nothing
new: she will strip you of your manhood and leave you helpless
reason: "unman" is a dated verb whose meaning (render impotent/powerless) isn't recoverable from sound alone for a listener who hasn't met the word before.

old: brought me water in a beautiful golden ewer
new: brought me water in a beautiful golden pitcher
reason: "ewer" is an archaic word for a water jug that most modern listeners won't recognize.

old: he was frightened by the severe reprimand I had given him
new: he was frightened by how close I had come to killing him
reason: The preceding paragraph shows Odysseus silently weighing whether to behead Eurylochus — no spoken reprimand is narrated — so "the severe reprimand" refers to a scene the listener never heard, a small continuity gap.

old: You will find it near the place where the rivers Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus (which is a branch of the river Styx) flow into Acheron
new: You will find it near the place where the rivers Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus — a branch of the river Styx — flow into the river Acheron
reason: Four unfamiliar proper nouns plus a parenthetical aside land in one sentence; very hard to track by ear even though the exact names aren't essential to following the instructions that follow (go to where the rivers meet).

old: fastening it with a golden girdle round her waist
new: fastening it with a golden belt round her waist
reason: "girdle" now most commonly means a woman's shaping undergarment; the older sense ("belt") is easy to momentarily misread as the modern one.
